summary: This document updates RFC 8253, which describes using TLS to secure PCEP (PCEPS). It adds restrictions on what PCEPS implementations do when they support more than one TLS version.

eli5.summary: Secure PCEP can speak more than one version of the secret language. This says which version to use when both sides know several.

questions: does pceps allow tls 1.3 early data
which tls version should pceps prefer
subtitle: Two extra TLS rules for secure PCEP: prefer the newest TLS version, and never use TLS 1.3 early data.

tldr.problem: RFC 8253 describes how to run PCEP over TLS (PCEPS), but it does not say what to do when an implementation supports several TLS versions, or whether TLS 1.3 early data may be used.
tldr.mechanism: This document adds two rules to the TLS connection establishment restrictions: implementations that support multiple TLS versions MUST prefer the latest one, and PCEPS implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 8253 and changes nothing else in it. Connection initiation, message framing, closure, certificate validation, peer identity and failure handling stay as RFC 8253 defines them.

facts.label: Version rule
facts.value: MUST prefer the latest TLS version

facts.label: Early data
facts.value: MUST NOT be used with TLS 1.3 or later

today: RFC 9916 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It updates RFC 8253 and has not been updated or obsoleted itself.

sections.title: What This Update Changes
sections.content:
PCEPS is the name for using TLS as a secure transport for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). RFC 8253 defines it and, in its Section 3.4, lists restrictions on how the TLS connection is established.

This document adds two restrictions to that list. It states that all other provisions of RFC 8253 are unchanged, including connection initiation, message framing, connection closure, certificate validation, peer identity and failure handling.
sections.eli5: There is already a rulebook for locking PCEP messages in a safe box. This note adds two small rules to it and leaves the rest alone.

sections.title: Preferring the Latest TLS Version
sections.content:
The first new rule applies to implementations that support more than one version of TLS, for example TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. They MUST prefer to negotiate the latest version of the TLS protocol.

The RFC points to Section 4.2.1 of RFC 9846 for how that version negotiation works.
sections.eli5: If both sides know old and new versions of the secret code, they must pick the newest one they share.

sections.title: No Early Data
sections.content:
The second rule says that PCEPS implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data. Early data, also called 0-RTT data, lets a TLS 1.3 client send data in the first flight of messages to a server.

The RFC explains why. Early data is permitted by TLS 1.3 only when client and server share a Pre-Shared Key (PSK). Its security properties are weaker than those of later TLS-protected data: it is not forward secret, and nothing protects against replay of early data between connections. TLS 1.3 can be used without early data.

The Security Considerations section adds that the security considerations of PCEP, TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3 and the TLS/DTLS recommendations in RFC 9325 apply as well.
sections.eli5: Sending your message before the secret handshake is done is risky, because someone could copy it and send it again. So PCEPS may not do that.
